newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs IDEC's Rituximab.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs IDEC's Rituximab.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisory panel on Friday unanimously voted that IDEC Pharmaceutical Corp's Rituxan (Rituximab) is effective and safe for treating non-Hodgkins lymphoma.
IDEC sought FDA approval for Rituximab, which will be co-promoted with Genentech Inc, in February 1997.
If approved by FDA, Rituximab will be the first-ever monoclonal therapeutic for cancer.
"This is an agent we should add to our armamentarium," said panel chairwoman Virginia Broudy of the University of Washington's School of Medicine.
Rituximab is meant for patients who have not responded to previous therapy for low-grade or follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL), which affect two-thirds of the 240,000 Americans with NHL.
This type of NHL is characterized by a series of remissions and relapses, with treatment becoming less effective with each succeeding illness, IDEC's Antonio Grillo-Lopez said.
Rituximab, tested in late-stage NHL patients, gave a response rate -- 48 percent -- comparable to chemotherapy or other NHL therapies, and with a better safety profile, Grillo-Lopez said.

In the pivotal trial, most of the 166 patients studied had stage 3 or 4 disease. Patients had significant previous treatments, with a median of two previous chemotherapy courses. Twenty-three had prior autologous bone marrow transplants (ABMT). Rituximab was given by infusion once a week for a month. Ninety-seven of a total of 203 patients studied had a complete or partial response. The FDA disagreed slightly, saying it counted 80 complete or partial responders. But the agency agreed with IDEC that 48 percent of patients responded.
Most patients had tumor shrinkage, with complete responders having 100 percent reduction. Half of the patients who responded are still in remission 13 months after therapy.

Because monoclonals are designed to target specific cells, they have held the promise of being safer and less toxic than chemotherapy. Rituximab, which combines mouse and human elements, caused mild side effects, Grillo-Lopez said. But the FDA said the effects were widespread. Eighty-five percent of patients experienced mild fever, chills, hypotension, and bronchospasm with the first infusion. Symptoms were relieved with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine. There were some cardiac problems, but these and other effects dissipated with subsequent infusions. Very few patients had opportunistic infections or depressed immunity as is common with chemotherapy.

And there was no immune response to Rituximab -- something that has hobbled previous attempts at monoclonal therapies. Panelist Charles August of the Miami Childrens Hospital said Rituximab was an "ice pick," when compared to the "hammer" of ABMT. But he cautioned the company against jumping to conclusions about lack of response to Rituximab, saying it may still appear.
